extracted.intended_audience: economists and policy researchers analyzing distributional effects of carbon pricing (public finance and climate policy analysts)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical general-equilibrium evaluation of the distributional incidence of carbon pricing, explicitly accounting for how government transfer programs are indexed (no indexing, partial, or full) and comparing household classification by annual income versus annual expenditures (proxy for lifetime income).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include both uses-side and sources-side incidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze both the uses side (burden from higher consumer prices of energy-intensive goods) and the sources side (changes in returns to factors of production such as capital and labor) when assessing distributional effects of carbon pricing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper emphasizes that the uses side is typically regressive because the fraction of income spent on energy-intensive goods falls with income, while the sources side can be progressive because carbon pricing reduces returns to capital (a larger share of high-income households' income). Both sides must be quantified and summed to obtain overall incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat government transfer indexing explicitly (no, partial, full)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide results for three treatments of transfer indexing: (1) ignore indexing entirely (no indexing), (2) assume 100% indexing of all transfers (full indexing), and (3) use partial indexing based on actual indexing rules across transfer programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare outcomes across these three treatments because analyses that ignore program-specific indexing may overestimate the regressivity of carbon pricing. The paper notes Rausch et al. (2010) assume 100% indexing; Browning (1985) provides theoretical justification for full indexing in some incidence frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household classification: annual income vs annual expenditures (proxy for permanent income)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify households either by annual income or by annual expenditures (the latter as a proxy for lifetime or permanent income) and report incidence under both classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The choice of income measurement strongly affects measured progressivity: using annual income shows stronger uses-side regressivity and a U-shaped sources-side burden; using annual expenditures can reduce measured regressivity on the uses side and show progressivity over the bottom half of the distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define dirty versus clean goods for mapping output to consumer prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Label consumer goods as 'dirty' or 'clean' to map output price changes into consumer price changes. The paper treats four expenditure types as dirty: electricity, natural gas, fuel oil and other fuels, and gasoline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice is motivated by pass-through estimates (e.g., Hassett et al. 2009) showing those four goods' prices rise substantially (8-13%) under a CO2 tax while most other categories rise <1%. Food is treated as a clean good here because the food industry's direct energy use is small and indirect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model choice and structural assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an analytical two-sector general equilibrium model (clean sector X and dirty sector Y) linearized around a baseline for small tax changes. Assumptions: two fixed factors mobile between sectors and fully employed, full information, certainty, perfect competition, constant returns to scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model is linearized by differentiating production, utility, budget, zero-profit, and resource constraints so that small changes in the pollution tax yield a solvable system of linear equations. State assumptions explicitly because they affect applicability (e.g., omission of market power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration and data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Calibrate the model to the U.S. economy using expenditure and income data from the 2008 Consumer Expenditure Survey (CEX) and capital income data from the 2007 Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report how imputed capital income affects ratios (the paper notes CEX expenditures/income statistics and differences with NIPA). Avoid arbitrary scaling unless justified; if scaling is applied, document its effect on relative burdens (authors note proportional scaling would not change relative burden results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue recycling / spending assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume pollution tax (or permit auction) revenue is spent on the two goods in the same proportions as consumer spending so that revenue reallocation has no impact on relative prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is analogous to Harberger (1962) and is used to isolate incidence effects. Make this assumption explicit since alternative revenue uses (lump-sum rebates, targeted transfers) alter incidence patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization and burden calculation procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Normalize group-specific uses-side burdens by subtracting the uses-side calculation for the entire sample (to remove arbitrary numeraire effects). For the sources side, reverse the sign so positive indicates income falling more than average. Sum output price, factor price, and transfer effects to compute normalized overall burden for each group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain sign conventions (positive means group’s ratio of expenditures to income increases more than average for uses side; positive on sources means income falls more than average). This ensures results are invariant to numeraire choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and model transfer program indexing by program category
rubrics_metrics.description: Disaggregate cash transfers into program categories (unemployment compensation (UC), TANF/public assistance, SNAP/food stamps, SSA/Social Security and Railroad Retirement, SSI, workers' compensation & veterans benefits) and assign indexing treatments per program (e.g., UC, TANF, SNAP treated as not indexed to energy; SSA/SSI/WC&VB treated as 100% indexed to CPI-W).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify program-level indexing choices: UC and TANF are not explicitly indexed; SNAP is indexed to a food-price-based 'thrifty food plan' (so not indexed to energy prices); SSA/SSI/WC&VB use CPI-W adjustments. Use program statutes and administrative practice to assign partial indexing shares for empirical exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external pass-through estimates when mapping sectoral tax changes to consumer price changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ literature estimates (e.g., Hassett et al. 2009) for how a CO2 tax translates into consumer price increases for specific goods to inform mapping from output price changes to consumer-level burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite empirical pass-through ranges (Hassett et al. find 8-13% increase for electricity, natural gas, fuel oil, gasoline under a $15/ton CO2 tax) and apply those to the dirty-good categories; document other goods' expected small price changes (<1%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for within-group heterogeneity and report distributional details
rubrics_metrics.description: Report that within deciles or expenditure groups there is heterogeneity (e.g., a third of the poorest expenditure decile receive no transfer income) and present distributional statistics or share of households that gain/lose within groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on decile averages; present the share of households protected by indexing versus those who still lose, and report magnitudes (the paper notes about 40% of poorest group have a large burden of ~0.8% of income while the rest have a relative gain ~0.7% of income).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct sensitivity analyses and consider model extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Test sensitivity to parameter values and consider model improvements such as adding more sectors, more final goods, intermediate goods, market power, and regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note that burdens on the sources side are sensitive to parameter values (e.g., substitution between capital and pollution). Extensions like market power in electric utilities or more detailed intermediate-good pass-through could materially affect incidence results.
